core_obligations: For an element of the closure of the set of topologically nilpotent elements and an open ideal, write the element as a sum of a topologically nilpotent element and an element of that ideal, choose a power of the former inside the ideal, and conclude that a power of the element lies in the ideal; hence the set is closed (proof lines 1147-1160).
Derive the first numbered assertion directly from the definitions of continuity and of topological nilpotence (proof lines 1160-1161).
Derive the second numbered assertion from the first together with closedness of the set of topologically nilpotent elements (proof lines 1161-1162).
Supply the verification that the set of topologically nilpotent elements is a radical ideal, which the author names as an exercise in the definitions and does not prove here (proof lines 1148-1150).
proof_roadmap: Closedness of the set of topologically nilpotent elements (proof lines 1147-1160).
Radicality, named as an exercise and left out (proof lines 1148-1150).
difficulty_reason: The lemma asserts that the set of topologically nilpotent elements of a linearly topologized ring is a closed radical ideal, that a continuous map sends topologically nilpotent elements to topologically nilpotent elements, and that the closure of the ideal generated by the image of a set of topologically nilpotent elements again consists of topologically nilpotent elements (statement lines 1133-1145). The proof isolates the two assertions it will use. It first shows closedness by a direct argument: an element of the closure of the set of topologically nilpotent elements differs from a topologically nilpotent element by an element of any given open ideal, so a suitable power of it lies in that ideal, which is exactly what topological nilpotence requires (proof lines 1147-1160). It then derives the two numbered assertions from that closedness, the first directly from the definitions and the second by combining the first with closedness of the set of topologically nilpotent elements (proof lines 1160-1162). The author states in passing that radicality is left as an exercise in the definitions, naming it as such; the claims of the lemma itself -- closedness and the two assertions -- are proved in the span, so the omission is recorded verbatim as an obligation rather than treated as an unproved block.
